strengths: Identifies an important and previously unexplored vulnerability in concept erasure methods, addressing a critical gap in AI safety research
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across six erasure methods, three threat scenarios, and multiple metrics with thorough ablation studies
Novel application of backdoor techniques to circumvent concept erasure, introducing multiple EEB variants with different attack points and mechanisms
Well-motivated threat model with clear assumptions; solid technical soundness demonstrated through systematic results
Clear presentation with effective figures and well-structured exposition; promises code release for reproducibility with detailed supplementary material provided
Timely contribution that advances understanding of adversarial robustness in generative models and will likely motivate more robust defense development
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily adapts existing backdoor and data poisoning techniques rather than introducing fundamentally new attack primitives
Threat model assumes white-box access and training data poisoning capability, which constrains practical threat realism and real-world applicability
Lacks concrete defense mechanisms or mitigation strategies; while identifying vulnerabilities is valuable, constructive solutions are minimal
Insufficient mechanistic analysis of why different erasure methods fail; missing analysis of failure mode commonalities or how combined erasure methods might improve robustness
No comprehensive evaluation of detection methods or defense strategies beyond brief mention of anomaly detection without empirical validation
Limited to text-to-image diffusion models and specific architectural versions; generalization to other generative models or domains not addressed

strengths: Addresses an important and timely security problem for concept erasure methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple erasure techniques (ESD, UCE, MACE, RECE, RECELER, ADVUNLEARN) and scenarios
Thorough supplementary material with detailed implementation information and ablation studies
Systematic testing across three distinct concept types (personal rights, objects, explicit content) with realistic metrics
Honest discussion of limitations and ethical implications of the work
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: EEB variants are straightforward applications of standard backdoor poisoning techniques to the erasure domain, lacking methodological innovation
Poorly justified threat model: Assumes researchers apply erasure to untrusted pre-trained models without adequate justification or discussion of quality control practices that would prevent this
Insufficient mechanistic understanding: Paper identifies that backdoors persist but doesn't explain why or what architectural properties enable evasion of different erasure methods
No constructive solutions: Section 4.6 on remedies is speculative and underdeveloped; paper identifies problems but offers almost no actionable defenses

Limited scope and generalization: Evaluation restricted to 10 celebrity identities, CIFAR-10 objects, and one sexual content dataset; unclear how findings transfer to other models (v3+), architectures, or concept types
Lacks statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance reporting despite claims of averaging across runs
Missing critical analyses: No comparison of attack vs. erasure computational costs; limited exploration of trigger robustness; insufficient analysis of detection feasibility
Crude evaluation metrics: ASR alone doesn't capture attack subtleties; doesn't analyze what happens under different threat scenarios (e.g., defender suspicion of backdoors)

strengths: Novel and well-motivated threat model: The Erasure Evasion Backdoor (EEB) concept is original and addresses a previously unexplored vulnerability where backdoors circumvent concept erasure methods. This is the first systematic study of this interaction.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough testing across 6 erasure methods (ESD, UCE, MACE, RECE, RECELER, ADVUNLEARN), 3 application domains (celebrity identity, object, explicit content), and multiple evaluation metrics demonstrates broad applicability of findings.

Rigorous methodology with extensive ablations: Multiple EEB variants, trajectory analysis, and ablation studies (Tables 8-9, Section D) clearly isolate which components are critical. Design choices are justified through systematic evaluation.

Strong reproducibility practices: Detailed supplementary material with implementation details, commitment to code release with responsible disclosure timeline, explicit prompts/templates in Section G, and clear hyperparameter specifications support reproducibility.

Practical significance for model safety: Findings have direct implications for deploying concept erasure methods and understanding their limitations. Important for the community as these methods become standard practice.

Clear presentation and visualization: Well-written with effective figures (Figures 1, 9) clearly illustrating threat model and attack persistence patterns. The paper is accessible despite technical content.
Responsible disclosure approach: Includes impact statement acknowledging potential misuse and proposes appropriate disclosure timelines, demonstrating research ethics considerations.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in attack techniques: While the threat model is novel, attack components largely combine existing methods (dirty-label poisoning, EvilEdit for cross-attention manipulation). The contribution is more in application than methodological innovation, reducing technical novelty.

Primarily negative results without proposed solutions: Paper identifies vulnerabilities but offers limited concrete defenses. Section 4.6 on remedies is superficial. Detection approaches (Figure 8) are underdeveloped. Leaves open how to robustly defend against EEB attacks.

Threat model assumptions need stronger justification: Assumes large-scale poisoned data publication and standard training procedures. Feasibility of coordinated attacks at scale and effectiveness against anomaly detection-aware training not thoroughly discussed.

Trigger robustness underexplored: Critical question of trigger variation tolerance is not systematically analyzed. How easily can triggers be distinguished from benign prompts? Sensitivity to trigger choice not thoroughly characterized.

Limited cross-architecture evaluation: Experiments primarily on SD v1.4. FLUX experiments (Section 4.5) are brief. Generalization to other model families and scales unclear, limiting scope of findings.

Detection defense evaluation insufficient: While Figure 8 shows weight watchers can detect anomalies, systematic evaluation of detection approaches is lacking. Practical detection reliability and adoption barriers not addressed.

Utility-security tradeoff not fully characterized: Paper identifies conflicts via α balancing but doesn't deeply explore the tradeoff space or provide guidance on acceptable utility degradation for improved robustness.
Trigger selection methodology not fully justified: Table 1 uses diverse but arbitrary triggers. Why these specific triggers? Sensitivity analysis for this critical component could be more thorough.

Missing coordination with model providers: No evidence of responsible disclosure to Hugging Face, OpenAI, or other platform operators who might benefit from understanding these vulnerabilities before exploitation.
